# Volume 5 — CHAPTER XIII. THE HOUSE ON THE HILL

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

A small, reliable spring, which was perpetually freezing cold and completely clear, sat within a specific hollow concealed by birches in the bottom corner of Fern Hollow close to the marsh. Its presence was not known by very many people. Naturally, the children from the manse and Hollowmere were aware of it, just as they were aware of all other details concerning the enchanted valley. Now and then they visited the spot for a drink, and it served as an ancient romantic fountain in numerous games they played. Nell was aware of it and cherished it since it somehow brought to mind the cherished Nymph’s Well located at Grey Shutters. Clementine Ainslie was aware of it; it served as her romantic fountain as well. Eighteen years previously, during a spring twilight, she had been seated behind it when young Martin Crawford hesitantly confessed his intense, youthful affection. She had murmured her own hidden feelings back to him, and beside the untamed forest spring, they exchanged kisses and vows. They never gathered beside it again—Martin embarked on his deadly journey shortly afterward; nevertheless, Clementine Ainslie perpetually considered it a holy place, sanctified by that timeless moment of adolescence and romance. Every time she went near the spot, she detoured to share a quiet rendezvous with a bygone dream—a dream whose agony had vanished long ago, retaining merely its lingering sweetness.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0000 }

The spring was concealed from view. One could walk by it within ten feet and not divine that it was there. Almost over it had fallen a large old pine sixty years ago. Nothing remained of that tree except a rotting trunk from which a dense growth of ferns emerged, creating a green canopy and a delicate barrier over the water. Next to it stood a maple with an strangely knotted and bent trunk that crawled along the earth briefly prior to rising skyward, thus shaping an unusual place to sit; and a ribbon of light smoke-blue asters had been draped around the depression by September.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0001 }

John Ashdown, while traveling back home from several pastoral calls near the Harbour head one evening by way of the cross-lots road through Fern Hollow, veered off to take a drink from the small spring. Just a short time prior, Edmund Carrow had pointed it out to him one afternoon, and they had engaged in an extended conversation while sitting on the maple bench. Beneath his entire shy and distant exterior, John Ashdown possessed a boyish heart. In his younger years, people had referred to him as Jack, although no resident of Glen St. Agnes would have ever credited such a thing. Edmund and he had drawn close to one another and conversed without restraint. Mr. Ashdown gained entry to certain locked and holy recesses of the youth’s spirit into which not even Izzy had ever peered. Starting from that warm moment, they were destined to be close companions, and Edmund realized he would not be intimidated by the clergyman ever again.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0002 }

“Prior to this, I didn't think one could genuinely come to know a clergyman,” he remarked to his mother that evening.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0003 }

John Ashdown took a drink from his thin white hand, which possessed a steel grip that invariably startled those who did not know it, and subsequently took a seat upon the maple bench. He felt no urge to return home quickly; the location was lovely, and he experienced mental exhaustion following a series of somewhat dull discussions with numerous kind yet foolish individuals. A rising moon appeared. At his exact location, Fern Hollow was haunted by the wind and watched over by stars alone, though joyous sounds of young people's voices and laughter drifted from its distant upper reach.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0004 }

The pale loveliness of the asters under the moon, the shimmer of the tiny spring, the gentle hum of the stream, and the swaying elegance of the brackens all cast a spell around John Ashdown. Church anxieties and religious dilemmas faded from his mind; the decades melted off him; he returned to being a youth studying theology, and the June roses were blossoming crimson and sweet-smelling upon the dusky, regal hair of his Cecilia. He remained seated and mused just like a youth. Then, during this favorable juncture, Clementine Ainslie left the small trail and paused next to him in that perilous, charm-casting spot. John Ashdown rose to his feet when she approached and looked upon her—truly looked upon her—for the initial time.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0005 }

On one or two occasions, he had come across her at his church and absently shaken her hand, just as he did with whoever he chanced to meet while walking down the aisle. Because the Ainslies belonged to the Episcopalian faith and were affiliated with a church in Kettlebridge, he had never run into her anywhere else, and there had never been a reason to visit them. Prior to this evening, had somebody inquired of John Ashdown regarding the appearance of Clementine Ainslie, he would have been completely unable to say. Yet, as she was revealed to him in the enchanting moonlight beside the spring, he was destined never to erase the memory of her.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0006 }

She definitely bore no resemblance whatsoever to Cecilia, the person who had continually represented his standard for female loveliness. While Cecilia had been petite, dark-haired, and full of life, Clementine Ainslie was imposing in height, light-complexioned, and serene; nevertheless, John Ashdown believed that a woman of such beauty had never before crossed his path.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0007 }

No hat covered her head, where her golden hair— hair possessing a warm gold hue described by Izzy Carrow as the shade of “molasses taffy”— sat fastened in smooth, tight braids; she possessed big, serene, blue eyes that constantly appeared to be brimming with goodwill, a lofty pale brow, and a exquisitely formed countenance.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0008 }

People invariably referred to Clementine Ainslie as a “sweet woman.” Her sweetness was so profound that not even her aristocratic, dignified demeanour ever caused her to be branded as “stuck-up,” a label that anyone else residing in Glen St. Agnes would have certainly received. Through life’s experiences, she had learned how to show bravery, exercise patience, express love, and grant forgiveness. Her eyes had followed the vessel carrying her beloved as it departed Seven Gulls Harbour, gliding into the setting sun. Nevertheless, despite her prolonged watch, she never beheld its return voyage. That prolonged waiting stripped the girlhood from her gaze, but she retained her youthful essence to an extraordinary extent. This was possibly owing to her constant retention of that feeling of joyful wonder toward existence that the majority of us abandon during our early years—a disposition that not merely imparted a youthful quality to Clementine herself, but also cast a delightful aura of youth over the mind of anybody engaged in conversation with her.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0009 }

Her beauty surprised John Ashdown, just as finding him there caught Clementine off guard. Finding a person beside that secluded spring had never crossed her mind, particularly not the hermit who lived at the Glen St. Agnes manse. The large stack of volumes she was bringing back from the Glen lending library nearly slipped from her arms, whereupon she uttered one of those minor untruths that even the most virtuous women occasionally resort to in order to hide her embarrassment.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0010 }

“I—I came for a drink,” she said, faltering slightly, replying to the solemn “good evening, Miss Ainslie” from Mr. Ashdown. She considered herself to be an unforgivable idiot, wishing she could give herself a shake. However, John Ashdown lacked vanity and recognized that an unexpected encounter with old Elder Clow would probably have startled her just as greatly. Because her embarrassment made him comfortable, he ceased being timid; moreover, in the moonlight, even the most bashful man can occasionally be fairly bold.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0011 }

“Allow me to fetch a cup for you,” he remarked with a smile. Nearby, a fractured blue cup lacking a handle was hidden beneath the maple by the Fern Hollow children, had he merely been aware of it; however, he was unaware, which led him to walk over to a birch-tree and peel off a piece of its white bark. Skillfully shaping this into a triangular container, he drew water from the spring and presented it to Clementine.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0012 }

Clementine accepted it and consumed all of it as a penalty for her lie, because she felt no thirst whatsoever, and consuming a rather substantial cup of water without being thirsty is a bit of a trial. Nevertheless, Clementine would come to cherish the recollection of that drink. During later years, she felt that it possessed a sacred quality. This might have been due to the actions of the minister upon receiving the returned cup from her. Bending down once more, he replenished the container and partook of it himself. His mouth touched the exact spot where Clementine had placed her own lips purely by chance, a fact of which Clementine was aware. Even so, the moment held a strange meaning for her. Both of them had partaken from the identical cup. A fleeting memory returned to her of an aged aunt who often remarked that if two individuals shared a drink like this, their future destinies would be connected in one way or another, be it for benefit or harm.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0013 }

With hesitation, John Ashdown gripped the cup. Unsure of how to handle the object, he considered throwing it as the sensible course of action, yet an odd reluctance stopped him from doing so. Reaching toward him, Clementine extended her hand to take it.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0014 }

“Would you allow me to keep it?” she asked. “You fashioned it with such skill. I have not witnessed a person craft a birch cup in that manner since my young brother was accustomed to making them many years in the past—prior to his death.”
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0015 }

“During my youth while camping out one summer, I picked up the skill to construct them from an old hunter,” remarked Mr. Ashdown. “Allow me to hold your books, Miss Ainslie.”
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0016 }

Surprised into telling a second untruth, Clementine stated that they were actually light. However, the minister claimed them from her with a rather authoritative manner, and the pair departed side by side. Never before had Clementine remained beside the valley spring without her thoughts turning to Martin Crawford. The secret rendezvous had been severed.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0017 }

A small side trail curved around the swamp before climbing the lengthy, forested height where Clementine made her home at the summit. Past that, amid the timber, the light of the moon was visible gleaming over the flat, warm-weather pastures. Nevertheless, the small trail remained dark and constricted. It was tightly hemmed in by trees, which are never entirely as welcoming to people once night arrives compared to when it is day. They retreat into themselves, separate from us. Their whispers and schemes are made in secret. Should they extend an arm toward us, its contact feels unwelcoming and hesitant. Individuals strolling among trees when it is dark invariably pull toward one another by impulse and without intending to, forging a physical and psychological pact facing particular foreign forces encircling them. As the two strolled, John Ashdown felt the fabric of Clementine’s gown brush against him. Even a distracted clergyman—who remained a youthful man despite his solid conviction that his romantic days were behind him—could not fail to feel the appeal of the darkness, the trail, and his fellow traveler.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0018 }

It is not entirely safe to assume that our time with life is over. Just when we believe our story has concluded, destiny often turns the page to reveal an additional chapter. These two individuals both believed their hearts were permanently attached to days gone by; nevertheless, each of them enjoyed their stroll up the hill immensely. Clementine considered the Glen pastor to be far less timid and mute than people had claimed. He appeared to experience no trouble conversing in a relaxed and open manner. Housewives in the Glen would have been astonished if they had listened to him. Yet a great number of Glen housewives spoke solely of rumor and how much eggs cost, and John Ashdown had no concern for such things. He spoke with Clementine about literature, music, global events, and a portion of his own past, discovering that she had the ability to comprehend and reply. Clementine, as it turned out, owned a volume that Mr. Ashdown had not perused and desired to read. She volunteered to give him the loan of it, and upon their arrival at the old hill residence, he stepped inside to retrieve it.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0019 }

The dwelling was an aged grey building covered in vines, with the living room lamp shining through them in a welcoming way. It overlooked the Glen, past the moonlit harbour that gleamed like silver, towards the sandhills and the lamenting sea. They entered across a garden where the scent of roses seemed perpetually present, despite the absence of blooming roses. A cluster of lilies stood by the entrance, a line of asters bordered both sides of the wide path, and a delicate network of firs topped the hill crest behind the home.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0020 }

“The entire world is right at your threshold in this place,” stated John Ashdown, taking a deep draft of air. “Such a vista—such a perspective! Now and then I feel suffocated down in the Glen. Air is available to breathe up here.”
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0021 }

“To-night is calm,” Clementine said with a laugh. “Your breath would be blown away if a wind were blowing. Up in this spot, we receive ‘a’ the airts the wind can blow’. Rather than the Harbour, Seven Gulls ought to be the name of this place.”
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0022 }

“I am fond of wind,” he remarked. “To my mind, a day lacking wind appears lifeless. I am aroused by a windy day.” He uttered a self-aware laugh. “A tranquil day causes me to slip into reveries. You are certainly aware of my repute, Miss Ainslie. Should I fail to acknowledge you at our subsequent encounter, do not attribute it to ill breeding. Kindly realize that it stems merely from preoccupation, pardon me—and address me.”
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0023 }

Harriet Ainslie was located in the sitting room as they entered. Placing her spectacles upon the volume she was in the middle of reading, she observed them with astonishment mixed with a different emotion. Nevertheless, she warmly shook hands with Mr. Ashdown, who took a seat and conversed with her while Clementine searched for his book.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0024 }

A decade older than Clementine, Harriet Ainslie bore so little resemblance to her that their sisterhood seemed scarcely credible. Dark and large of build, she possessed black hair, bushy black eyebrows, and eyes that matched the transparent, slaty blue of gulf waters during a northerly breeze. Although her expression appeared somewhat severe and off-putting, her true disposition was quite cheerful, marked by a robust, bubbling laugh and a rich, smooth, agreeable voice that carried a hint of male quality. On an earlier occasion, she had observed to Clementine that she would genuinely enjoy conversing with that Presbyterian minister at the Glen, aiming to test whether he could muster anything to say to a female if backed into a corner. Having found her opportunity at present, she engaged him regarding global affairs. Being an avid reader, Miss Harriet had recently finished consuming a volume concerning the Kaiser of Germany, and she requested that Mr. Ashdown share his thoughts about him.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0025 }

“A perilous person,” he replied.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0026 }

“I take your word for it!” agreed Miss Harriet. “Pay attention to what I say, Mr. Ashdown, because that person will end up in a battle eventually. He craves it. He will cause an absolute sensation.”
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0027 }

“I scarcely believe he would aimlessly provoke a major conflict, if that is what you are implying,” Mr. Ashdown remarked. “The time for such behavior has passed.”
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0028 }

“God bless you, no, it has not,” Harriet boomed. “Not a day passes without people and countries acting foolishly and resorting to fighting. We are not that close to the millennium, Mr. Ashdown, a fact you realize just as well as I. Regarding this Kaiser, pay attention to what I say, he will cause a great deal of difficulty”—and with her slender digit, Miss Harriet jabbed her book forcefully. “Indeed, unless he is stopped early on, he will cause difficulty. It will happen in our lifetime—both you and I will witness it, Mr. Ashdown. And who will stop him? England ought to, yet she will not. Who will stop him? Answer me that, Mr. Ashdown.”
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0029 }

Although Mr. Ashdown was unable to inform her, they engaged in a conversation regarding German militarism that continued well past the time Clementine located the volume. Clementine remained silent, sitting instead in a small rocking chair behind Harriet while thoughtfully petting a prominent black cat. John Ashdown pursued large game in Europe alongside Harriet, yet his gaze fell upon Clementine more frequently than upon Harriet, an observation that Harriet did not miss. Following Clementine’s departure to accompany him to the doorway and her subsequent return, Harriet stood up and stared at her with an air of accusation.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0030 }

“Clementine Ainslie, it seems to me that man intends to court you.”
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0031 }

Clementine trembled. She felt as though Harriet’s words were a physical strike. They stripped away all the charm of the enjoyable evening. Nevertheless, she refused to allow Harriet to perceive how much she was wounded by it.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0032 }

“Rubbish,” she uttered, giving a chuckle that sounded slightly forced. “Harriet, you imagine a suitor for me behind every tree. Why, he disclosed everything regarding his wife to me this evening—what she meant to him—how devoid of meaning the world became after she died.”
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0033 }

“Well, he might court in that manner,” Harriet replied. “I gather that men employ all sorts of methods. However, Clementine, remember what you promised.”
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0034 }

“I have no cause to either put it out of my mind or keep it in mind,” Clementine remarked, somewhat tiredly. “Harriet, you do not remember that I am an old maid. My being yet youthful and flourishing and perilous is nothing more than your sisterly fantasy. Mr. Ashdown simply desires to be a friend—should he even desire that much. Long prior to his return to the manse, he will have forgotten the two of us.”
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0035 }

“I do not mind if you are friendly with him,” admitted Harriet, “however, keep in mind that it cannot exceed friendship. Widowers always make me suspicious. Romantic notions regarding friendship are not typical for them. Business is what they are likely to mean. Regarding this Presbyterian man, why is he considered shy by people? Absent-minded he might be, yet he is not the least bit shy—his absent-mindedness was so great that he neglected to bid me goodnight as you began walking to the door alongside him. Furthermore, he possesses intelligence. Very few men in these parts are capable of speaking sensibly to a person. The evening was enjoyable to me. Seeing him again would not bother me. Nonetheless, Clementine, remember—no philandering, no philandering.”
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0036 }

Harriet frequently cautioned Clementine against flirting whenever she merely conversed for five minutes with any eligible man aged between eighteen and eighty. The admonition had constantly provoked genuine laughter from her in the past. On this occasion, far from entertaining her, it caused her slight irritation. Who harbored any desire to philander?
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0037 }

“Harriet, stop being so silly,” she remarked with an unusual sharpness while grabbing her lamp. Leaving without bidding goodnight, she ascended the stairs.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0038 }

Harriet, expressing doubt, shook her head while her gaze fell upon the black cat.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0039 }

“Why is she in such a bad mood, St. Laurence?” she inquired. “I have always been told, Laurence, that you only yell when you are struck. However, Saint, she gave her word—she gave her word, and members of our family, the Ainslies, never break a promise. Therefore, Laurence, his desire to flirt will be of no consequence. She gave her word. I will not be anxious.”
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0040 }

In her room upstairs, Clementine remained seated for a lengthy period, gazing through the window past the garden bathed in moonlight toward the gleaming, far-off harbour. A indistinct feeling of distress and restlessness washed over her. All at once, she grew weary of faded dreams. Meanwhile, out in the garden, a brief, sudden gust of wind dispersed the petals of the final red rose. Summer had ended—autumn had arrived.
{: #nw-v05-c13-p0041 }
